overview: The Moscow-centred Russian state became a tsardom when Ivan IV was crowned in 1547. It endured a severe succession crisis, then continued under the Romanovs. Expansion, printing and skilled crafts accompanied deep social inequality. Peter I adopted the imperial title in 1721, marking its transition into the Russian Empire.

periods.title: Tsars and a succession crisis
periods.summary: Ivan IV’s coronation established the tsar’s title; the early seventeenth century brought famine, disorder and competing rulers.

periods.title: The early Romanovs
periods.summary: Mikhail Romanov’s election began a new dynasty. The 1649 law code strengthened hereditary serfdom.

periods.title: Peter’s reign and an imperial title
periods.summary: Peter I’s reign culminated in victory over Sweden and adoption of the title emperor in 1721.

items.text: Ivan IV’s coronation took place in the Kremlin’s Dormition Cathedral on 16 January 1547. Religious ritual and royal regalia presented his authority as sacred. The ceremony matters because the map’s imported label begins earlier, when Moscow’s ruler still held the grand-princely title.

Saint Basil’s Cathedral was built in Moscow from 1555 to 1561 to commemorate victory over the Kazan Khanate. Its clustered churches turned a military conquest into a major architectural commission. The complex changed afterwards; the church dedicated to Basil the Blessed was added in 1588.

The early seventeenth-century Time of Troubles brought famine, political breakdown, rival claimants and foreign intervention. In 1613 an assembly chose the young Mikhail Romanov as tsar. Establishing a dynasty did not instantly repair ruined farms and towns, but it restored a continuing line of rulers.

The law code adopted in 1649 tied privately owned peasants and their descendants to their landlords’ estates. It also removed time limits on pursuing fugitives. For these families, moving away to seek a better life could bring forced return; the state’s growing strength did not mean growing freedom for everyone.

During the seventeenth century, Russian expeditions crossed Siberia and reached the Pacific. Fur tribute, called yasak, helped drive this expansion. Historian Denis Shaw emphasizes coercion and violent conflict as well as journeys and geographical knowledge: these were inhabited lands whose peoples faced new demands from an expanding state.

Ivan Fedorov and Petr Mstislavets completed the Apostle in 1564, Moscow’s first precisely dated printed book. It contained biblical Acts and Epistles and took about eleven months to produce. The edition carried features useful for church reading as well as reading at home or in a monastic cell.

Printing red and black on the same page required careful work. For the Apostle, the letters intended to print in red were raised above the rest, printed, then removed before the black text was added. A misaligned sheet could spoil the effect; attractive pages depended on workshop skill.

Moscow’s Kislovskaya quarter housed suppliers of sour cabbage, soaked apples, pickled cucumbers and kvass for the court. Preserving food made winter supplies possible. Archaeologists found cellar pits in the neighbourhood, connecting the written history of its food workers with the spaces in which they worked.

Seventeenth-century layers in that quarter yielded green-glazed stove tiles, a miniature ceramic jug and an enamelled copper-alloy cross. These finds bring colour into an otherwise earth-brown excavation. They also help distinguish the tsardom’s neighbourhood from the larger eighteenth- and nineteenth-century estates built over it.

Kolomenskoye’s water tower, built in the 1670s, raised water from a source beneath it to a large barrel above. Water then travelled through wooden pipes to palace buildings. Researchers describe pumps or a bucket mechanism: even a royal water supply needed somebody’s machinery to do the lifting.

In 1654 the Apothecary Chancery organized a school to train medical practitioners. Thirty musketeers and musketeers’ sons were assigned to foreign medical teachers, with interpreters helping lessons along. Graduates served with army regiments or the chancery. This was a small specialist programme, far from healthcare for every household.

Karion Istomin’s 1696 primer taught letters, syllables, numbers and religious texts. Only twenty copies were printed for an edition intended for Tsarevich Alexei. A surviving proof copy bears editorial corrections, while red letters in a poem spell out the author’s name. Even a royal schoolbook needed proofreading.

The primer addresses “к юношам учитися хотящим”, literally “to young people wishing to learn”. This is its historical Church Slavonic wording in the library’s normalized Cyrillic transcription, rather than a reproduction of the printed letter shapes. The greeting makes a seventeenth-century textbook sound pleasantly welcoming.

ending.text: Peter I accepted the title emperor in 1721 after the Treaty of Nystad ended the Northern War with Sweden. The tsardom became the Russian Empire through a change of political title and institutions, not the disappearance of its population. The imported 1530 to 1783 map range spans both earlier and later phases.
